1.title: STAKEHOLDER MANAGEMENT & COMMUNICATION
1.text: Welcome to Module 11. Architecture isn't just a technical exercise — it succeeds or fails on people. The stakeholders who fund it, use it, build it, and are affected by it ultimately determine whether your architecture thrives or gathers dust. This module covers TOGAF's stakeholder management technique: how to identify the right people, understand their positions, decide how to engage each one, and communicate effectively throughout. The four-step process and the Power/Interest grid are the two things the exam loves here, so let's give them proper attention.

1.title: Module Overview & Learning Objectives
1.text: Here's the plan. You'll explain why stakeholder management matters so much. You'll walk through the four steps of the process. You'll use the Power/Interest grid and its four engagement strategies. You'll distinguish the Visible team from the Invisible team — a TOGAF distinction worth knowing. And you'll describe the Stakeholder Map and the Communications Plan, both of which we first met back in Phase A. The two highest-value things to lock in are the four steps and the Power/Interest grid. Get those solid and this module is comfortably in hand.

1.title: Why Stakeholder Management Matters
1.text: Let's start with why this matters. The most successful architectures are the ones that genuinely address stakeholder concerns — it's right there in the standard's executive overview. Support from powerful stakeholders helps the engagement win more resources, which makes the whole architecture effort far more likely to succeed. And engaging early lets you anticipate likely reactions and turn potential critics into advocates before opposition hardens. TOGAF treats this as an important ADM Technique, used heavily in Phase A and then maintained throughout. So the headline is simple: stakeholder management is about winning support and surfacing concerns early, while you can still act on them.

1.title: Benefits of Stakeholder Management
1.text: Let's spell out the benefits, because the exam sometimes asks for them directly. First, powerful stakeholders get to shape the architecture early, which means a better fit and far fewer nasty surprises later. Second, their support secures the resources and the momentum the project needs. Third, communicating early and often means stakeholders actually understand what you're doing — and people support what they understand. And fourth, you can anticipate likely reactions and build your response into the plan rather than scrambling later. Four benefits, easy to remember as a cluster: resources, early shaping, understanding, and anticipation. Each one tilts the odds toward success.

1.title: The 4 Steps of Stakeholder Management
1.text: Here's the core process — four steps, and the order is logical. Step one, identify your stakeholders. Step two, classify their positions — understand where each one stands. Step three, determine your stakeholder management approach, which is where the Power/Interest grid comes in. And step four, tailor your engagement deliverables to each group. So the flow is: find them, understand them, decide how to engage them, then produce the right things for them. Identify, Classify, Determine approach, Tailor deliverables. Know that order — the exam can ask you to sequence them.

1.title: Step 1 — Identify Stakeholders
1.text: Step one, identifying stakeholders, means working out everyone who's affected by the architecture, who has influence or power over it, or who has an interest in its success or failure. TOGAF suggests a set of probing questions: who gains and who loses from this change? Who makes the decisions? Who controls the resources? Who has the specialist skills the project needs? And here's a warning the standard stresses: don't over-focus on the formal organization chart. Informal stakeholder groups and influencers can be just as powerful as the formal ones — sometimes more so. And ultimately, even when a stakeholder is an organization, you communicate with individuals, so identify the right people by name.

1.title: The Visible & Invisible Teams
1.text: TOGAF draws a neat distinction worth remembering. The Visible team is made up of those obviously associated with the project or change — the people everyone naturally thinks of. The Invisible team is made up of those who must make a real contribution for the project to succeed, but who are not obviously associated with it — think of the providers of support services who quietly keep everything running. The lesson is that you must identify and manage both. The Invisible team is easy to overlook precisely because it's invisible, and yet its members are often critical to success. So when you brainstorm stakeholders, deliberately ask: who's contributing that we're not seeing?

1.title: Sample Stakeholder Analysis
1.text: To help you get started, TOGAF provides a sample stakeholder analysis that distinguishes twenty-two types of stakeholder, grouped into five broad categories. Now, the important caveat: this is illustrative, not prescriptive. Any particular architecture project may have more, fewer, or entirely different stakeholders, and they may fall into more, fewer, or different categories. It's a starting point to spark your thinking, not a fixed checklist to apply blindly. For the exam, the figure to remember is twenty-two stakeholder types in five categories — and the understanding that it's a sample you tailor, in keeping with TOGAF's whole tailoring philosophy.

1.title: Step 2 — Classify Stakeholder Positions
1.text: Step two is to classify stakeholder positions — to develop a genuine understanding of your most important stakeholders and record it for reference. For each key stakeholder, you capture several things: their ability to disrupt the change; their current understanding versus the understanding they'll need; their current commitment versus the commitment they'll need; and the support required from them. You're essentially assessing each person's readiness to behave supportively. The value is that it shows you the gap — where someone is now versus where they need to be. So classification tracks understanding, commitment, and ability to disrupt, each measured as current versus required. That gap is what your engagement then works to close.

1.title: Step 3 — Determine the Approach (Power/Interest)
1.text: Step three is where you decide how to engage. You work out each stakeholder's power, influence, and interest, and then you map them onto a Power/Interest grid. That grid does something clever: it doesn't just classify people, it indicates the engagement strategy to adopt for each one. It instantly reveals which stakeholders are likely to be blockers or critics, and which are likely to be advocates and supporters — so you can focus your energy on the key individuals. As the diagram shows, power runs up the vertical axis and interest runs across the horizontal, dividing stakeholders into four quadrants. Let's look at those quadrants, because they're prime exam material.

1.title: The Four Power/Interest Quadrants
1.text: Here are the four quadrants. High power and high interest puts a stakeholder in the Key Players quadrant — these you manage closely. High power but low interest means Keep Satisfied — they could derail you if they became unhappy, but they don't want the detail. Low power but high interest means Keep Informed — they care, and they can make useful advocates. And low power with low interest means Minimal Effort — you simply monitor them. The two extremes anchor it: high-high gets the most attention as Key Players, and low-low gets the least as minimal effort. Picture the grid and put the most important people in the top-right.

1.title: Engagement Strategies Explained
1.text: Let's expand each strategy, because matching quadrant to strategy is a classic question format. Key Players, high power and high interest — engage them fully and manage them closely; these are your most important relationships. Keep Satisfied, high power but low interest — keep them content, but don't bury them in detail they don't want. Keep Informed, low power but high interest — keep them updated, because their enthusiasm makes them useful advocates who can champion your cause. And Minimal Effort, low power and low interest — monitor them with the least effort, but don't ignore them entirely in case their position shifts. Four quadrants, four distinct strategies — learn them as pairs.

1.title: Step 4 — Tailor Engagement Deliverables
1.text: Step four is to tailor your engagement deliverables. Here you identify the specific catalogs, matrices, and diagrams that the architecture engagement needs to produce and validate with each stakeholder group. This is where stakeholder management links straight back to views and viewpoints from Module 10 — you tailor the views to each group's particular concerns. The payoff is that it lets stakeholders verify, for themselves, that the architecture initiative will actually address their concerns. So engagement deliverables are simply the artifacts and views you deliberately choose to satisfy each stakeholder group. You're not producing everything for everyone — you're producing the right things for the right people.

1.title: The Stakeholder Map
1.text: The key output of all this work is the Stakeholder Map. It records, for the engagement, each stakeholder's level of involvement, their concerns, and the viewpoints that are relevant to them. We first met it back in Phase A, where it's created — and crucially, it's not a one-time artifact. The Stakeholder Map is updated throughout the ADM as the engagement progresses and new stakeholders come to light. So for the exam, anchor two facts: the Stakeholder Map is created in Phase A, and it's maintained across the whole cycle. It's a living document, not a snapshot you file and forget.

1.title: Communication — The Communications Plan
1.text: Stakeholder management is incomplete without communication, and TOGAF's instrument for that is the Communications Plan — which, like the Stakeholder Map, comes from Phase A. The Communications Plan defines where, how, and when the architects will communicate with stakeholders. It targets the various affinity groupings and communities you've identified, and its purpose is to keep stakeholders engaged and informed as the architecture evolves. One specific exam fact to file away: the Communications Plan is developed as part of the Statement of Architecture Work in Phase A. So the plan to talk to people is baked into the very document that authorizes the architecture work.

1.title: Stakeholders, Concerns, Views — The Chain
1.text: Let's connect this module back to the last one, because they form a single chain. Stakeholders have concerns. Viewpoints are selected to frame those concerns. And views are created to demonstrate that the concerns have been addressed. Stakeholder management is what feeds this chain — it identifies the right people and establishes their priorities, so the rest of the chain has something to work with. So the full sequence reads: stakeholder management, then concerns, then viewpoints, then views. Modules 10 and 11 are really two halves of one story — the structural half and the human half. Keep them linked in your mind.

1.title: When Stakeholder Management Happens
1.text: When does all this happen in the ADM? Primarily in Phase A, where you identify stakeholders and build both the Stakeholder Map and the Communications Plan. But it doesn't stop there. It's updated in every phase, because new stakeholders emerge as the engagement moves forward — for instance, fresh stakeholders often surface during Opportunities and Solutions, or during Migration Planning, as the work becomes more concrete. So stakeholder management is a continuous discipline, not a one-off task. It begins in Phase A and is refreshed throughout. If a question implies it's done once and finished, that's the trap — it's an ongoing activity.

1.title: Common Exam Traps
1.text: Let's clear the traps. One: "only formal or senior stakeholders matter" — no, informal influencers and the Invisible team matter just as much, sometimes more. Two: "low power, low interest means manage closely" — no, that quadrant is minimal effort; it's the high-high Key Players you manage closely. Three: "the Stakeholder Map is built in Phase G" — no, it's built in Phase A. And four: "stakeholder management is a one-time task" — no, it's updated throughout the ADM. The two things to over-learn so these traps can't catch you are the four steps and the Power/Interest grid quadrants. Drill those and you're safe.

1.title: Key Numbers & Quick Facts (Cheat Sheet)
1.text: Your cheat-sheet. Stakeholder management has four steps. The sample analysis distinguishes twenty-two stakeholder types in five categories. The mapping tool is the Power/Interest grid. High power plus high interest equals Key Players, managed closely; low power plus low interest equals minimal effort, just monitored. There are two team types — Visible and Invisible. The key output is the Stakeholder Map, from Phase A. And the communication tool is the Communications Plan, also from Phase A. Capture this card — between the four steps and the grid, it covers the module's most-tested facts.

1.title: Module Summary
1.text: Let's recap. Stakeholder management wins support and ensures concerns are addressed — it's a people discipline at the heart of a technical framework. The four steps are Identify, Classify, Determine approach, and Tailor deliverables. The Power/Interest grid sorts stakeholders into Key Players, Keep Satisfied, Keep Informed, and Minimal Effort, each with its own engagement strategy. Watch carefully for the Invisible team and for informal influencers. And both the Stakeholder Map and the Communications Plan originate in Phase A and are maintained throughout the ADM. People first, then the architecture serves them well.

1.title: Memory Hook
1.text: Two quick memory hooks. For the four steps, remember I-C-D-T: Identify, Classify, Determine approach, Tailor. And for the grid, remember "power up, interest across" — so the top-right corner, high power and high interest, is always your Key Players, and it always gets the most attention. I-C-D-T for the steps, top-right for the most important people. Those two little anchors will carry you through almost every stakeholder question the exam can ask. Simple, but they hold up well when the pressure is on.

1.title: Bridge to Module 12
1.text: So where to next? Notice how much of what we've discussed — stakeholder agreements, the contracts that bind delivery teams, the compliance that keeps everyone honest — ultimately sits under one umbrella: Architecture Governance. That's the subject of Module 12, where we'll cover the Architecture Board, the governance framework, and architecture compliance. The connecting idea is that governance is the machinery that holds stakeholders, contracts, and standards together and makes them stick. Having looked at the people, we now look at how their agreements are enforced. On to governance.

1.title: Quick Self-Check
1.text: A quick self-check. From memory: can you list the four steps in order? Can you draw the Power/Interest grid and correctly label all four quadrants with their strategies? Can you define the Invisible team? And can you say which phase first produces the Stakeholder Map? If the grid feels at all uncertain, go back and re-watch slides eleven and twelve — the quadrants and their strategies. That grid is the single most likely thing to appear from this module, and it's very answerable once the four labels are second nature. Take a moment to picture it now.

1.title: Why This Connects Everywhere
1.text: Before the questions, let me stress how this module threads through the whole framework. Phase A's Stakeholder Map drives the viewpoints and views from Module 10. Governance, coming up in Module 12, enforces the agreements you make with stakeholders, via contracts. And at the deepest level, the entire ADM exists to address stakeholder concerns — that's the purpose statement we started the course with. So stakeholders aren't a side topic; they're the reason the architecture exists at all. Keep them central in your thinking, and a surprising number of exam questions across other modules suddenly make more sense. People are the through-line.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question 1. What are the four steps of the TOGAF stakeholder management process, in order? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. Identify stakeholders, Classify positions, Determine approach, Tailor engagement deliverables The four steps are Identify stakeholders → Classify stakeholder positions → Determine the stakeholder management approach (Power/Interest grid) → Tailor engagement deliverables. Order matters: you find them, understand them, decide how to engage, then choose what to produce for them.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question 2. On the Power/Interest grid, how should you engage a stakeholder with high power and high interest? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is C. Manage them closely as Key Players High power and high interest places a stakeholder in the Key Players quadrant — they should be managed closely and engaged fully. High power but low interest means "keep satisfied"; low power but high interest means "keep informed"; low-low means "minimal effort."

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question 3. What is the "Invisible team" in TOGAF stakeholder management? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. Those who must make a real contribution to success but are not obviously associated with the project The Invisible team consists of stakeholders who must contribute for the project to succeed but are not obviously associated with it — for example, providers of support services. They're easy to overlook, which is exactly why TOGAF highlights them alongside the "Visible team."

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question 4. In which ADM phase is the Stakeholder Map first created? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. Phase A: Architecture Vision The Stakeholder Map is first produced in Phase A, as part of identifying stakeholders and their concerns. It is then updated throughout the rest of the ADM as new stakeholders emerge.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question 5. When classifying stakeholder positions, which factors does TOGAF suggest recording for each key stakeholder? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. Ability to disrupt, current vs required understanding, current vs required commitment, and required support Classifying positions records each key stakeholder's ability to disrupt the change, their current versus required understanding, their current versus required commitment, and the required support. This reveals where you need to move each stakeholder from where they are to where they need to be.
